 Summary
 The Hanford Site stores an estimated 56 million gallons of mixed radioactive and chemically
 hazardous waste in large underground tanks. In support of the Direct Feed Low-Activity Waste
 (DFLAW) program for expediting Hanford tank waste supernate treatment, laboratory-scale ion
 exchange processing using prototypic unit operations was conducted on AW-105 tank waste at
 the Pacific Northwest National Laboratory Radiochemical Processing Laboratory.

 This report describes the batch contact testing for tanks AN-107 and AP-105 to help evaluate
 CST performance on tanks waste supernate after processing it in the ion exchange columns to
 strip 137Cs. The volume of each supernate was adjusted to six Na concentrations (3.5 M, 4.5 M,
 5.5 M, 6.0 M, 7.0 M, and 8.0 M Na) which were then spiked with 133Cs at four concentrations
     (1.7E-04 M, 4.0E-04 M, 1.0E-03 M, and 1.7E-02 M Cs). Table S-1 provides a summary of the Kd
 and Q values for each tank waste matrix. All matrices showed a linear decrease in Kd with
 increasing Na concentration. The Kd and Q values for tanks AN-107 and AP-105 were compared
 to values from AP-107 results conducted in a separate study. Results from this work show slightly
 higher Kd values and significantly lower Q values than the AP-107 data.

Introduction 1

Introduction 2

 1.0 Introduction
 Hanford Tank Waste Operations and Closure (H2C) is the tank operations contactor for the U.S.
 Department of Energy (DOE) Hanford Field Office on the Hanford Site. The Hanford Site stores
 an estimated 56 million gallons of mixed radioactive and chemically hazardous waste in large
 underground tanks. In support of the Direct Feed Low-Activity Waste (DFLAW) Program, DOE
 deployed a strategy to pretreat supernate waste at tank farms and send it directly to Hanford’s
 Waste Treatment and Immobilization Plant (WTP) Low-Activity Waste (LAW) facility for
 vitrification. To accommodate this strategy, DOE and H2C developed a two-phased approach.
 The first phase consisted of the deployment of a Tank Side Cesium Removal (TSCR) system
 located at AP Farm as a part of the TSCR Demonstration Project, which began operations in
 January 2022. This system provides the initial feed for hot commissioning of the WTP-LAW
 facility. The second phase will consist of the deployment of a higher capacity pretreatment system
 called the Advanced Modular Pretreatment System (AMPS) that can deliver sufficient feed for two
 melters in the WTP-LAW facility. Decanted tank waste supernate will be pretreated using AMPS
 to meet the WTP LAW Facility waste acceptance criteria (WAC). Specific to 137Cs, this
 requirement is <3.18E-5 Ci 137Cs/mole of Na.

 The goal of this work was to test the effectiveness of CST to remove Cs from AN-107 and AP-
       105 supernate at six Na concentrations (3.5, 4.5, 5.5, 6.0, 7.0, and 8.0 M Na).

 H2C funded PNNL to conduct testing with AP-105 tank waste under the Task 2 of the WRPS
 statement of work FY 2022 Radioactive Waste Test Platform Testing, Rev. 2, Requisition 351656,
 dated July 21, 2022. Testing with AN-107 tank waste was conducted under the WRPS statement
 of work Tank 241-AN-107 Large Volume Sample Collection to Support Platform Testing, Phase
 2, FY23, Rev. 0, Requisition 366862, dated June 29, 2023. There are no deviations from the
 statement of work.

Quality Assurance 4

 3.0 Test Conditions
 This section describes the CST media, AN-107 tank waste, AP-105 tank waste, and batch contact
 conditions. All testing was conducted in accordance with a test plan prepared by PNNL and
 approved by the tank farm contractor.

 3.1 CST media
 The CST ion exchange media used in this study was procured by WRPS as ten 5-gallon buckets
       (149 kg total) of IONSIV R9140-B CST, Product 8056202-999, Lot No. 2002009604 from
 Honeywell UOP LLC (Des Plaines, IL, USA). Details of the procurement and material properties
 can be found elsewhere (Fiskum et al. 2019). The CST was sieved through a #30 sieve assembly
 and pretreated by contacting with 0.1 M NaOH to remove colloidal fines.

 3.2 AN-107 Tank Waste Sample
 The tank farm contractor collected multiple samples (36 at nominally 250 mL each) from the AN-
 107 Hanford tank in August and September of 2023. Characterization of the AN-107 samples are
 described elsewhere (Westesen et al. 2024). A source of ~5.5 M Na AN-107 was received for this
 study. The AN-107 source was separated into six aliquots for Na concentration adjustment. The
 aliquots were either diluted with DI water or heated to adjust the volume for the appropriate Na
 concentration for batch contact feed. The batch contact (BC) feed solutions were transferred into
 poly bottles to record gross mass. Sub-aliquots (2 mL) of each AN-107 BC feed were analyzed to
 determine 137Cs content and Na concentration (ASR 2094).

 were either diluted with DI water or heated to adjust the volume to achieve the appropriate Na
 concentration for batch contact feed. The BC feed solutions were transferred into poly bottles to

 3.4 Batch contact conditions
 Batch contact experiments with AN-107 and AP-105 effluents were conducted to evaluate Cs
 loading at various Na concentrations. Stock solutions of 0.753 M (100 mg/mL) and 9.98E-02 M
 (13.3 mg/mL) 133CsNO3 were prepared by dissolving the nitrate salt in a tared volumetric flask and
 diluted with DI water. Stocks of 133Cs with known concentration and density were used for spiking
 of both AN-107 and AP-105 effluent samples. Four 50 mL centrifuge tubes were prepared for
       each BC feed solution to achieve 1.7E-04, 4.0E-04, 1.0E-03, and 1.7E-02 M Cs. The 0.084 M
 133Cs stock was spike in various volumes to 3 of the 4 centrifuge tubes per feed solution. The

 fourth centrifuge tube was spiked with the 0.753 M 133Cs stock. A 30 mL aliquot of each feed
 solution was added to its appropriate 50 mL centrifuge tube. The solutions were prepared
 gravimetrically, and exact volumes were calculated from mass and density measurements.

 A nominal 0.075 g (dry mass basis) aliquot of CST was measured into 20 mL vials and used to
 determine the dry mass of the exchanger. The F-factor was measured at nominally 105 °C with a
 value of 0.4262 for AN-107 and 0.3737 for AP-105 BC testing, respectively. The lower-than-
 expected F-factor is likely due to the CST not being fully dry before F-factor testing. This F-factor
 was used to calculate the target mass of CST for the batch contact tests. F-factor samples were
 again collected in duplicate, bracketing batch contact sample collection. The average F-factor
 was measured at 105 °C with an average value of 0.5404 for AN-107 and 0.5181 for the AP-105
 BC testing, respectively. These values were used to measure the dry mass of CST for their
 respective tank waste samples.

 Aliquots (15 mL) of the BC feed solutions were added to the appropriate vials (in duplicate); the
 exact volume transferred was calculated from net solution mass and density. The solution-to-
 mass phase ratio was averaged 193 ± 4 and 141 ± 1 for AN-107 and AP-105, respectively.

 Batch contact tests were conducted subsequently; first the AN-107 then with AP-105. All samples
 were contacted at ambient temperature on a large orbital shaker set to 200 RPM. The temperature
 was monitored using a vial of DI water co-located with each sample set.

 After contact, 2 mL of the supernate was removed and filtered through a 0.45 µm pore size nylon
 syringe filter and transferred to a glass vial for gamma energy analysis (GEA). The 137Cs activity
 measured by GEA in pre- and post-contacted solutions was used to determine the total Cs
 exchange. Analysis and data reduction were conducted using the methods previously reported
 (Fiskum et al. 2019a). The isotherm data were fitted to a Freundlich/Langmuir hybrid equilibrium
       fit (Hamm et al. 2002).

 The batch distribution coefficients were calculated according to Eq. (3.1).

 3.5 Sample analysis
 Cesium load performance was determined from the 137Cs measured in the collected samples
 relative to the native 137Cs in each respective feed. The samples collected were analyzed directly
 to determine the 137Cs concentration using GEA.

 The ASO was responsible for the preparation and analysis of appropriate analytical batch and
 instrument quality control samples and for providing any additional processing to the sub-samples
 that might be required (e.g. acid digestion, radiochemical separations, dilutions). All analyses
 were conducted by the ASO according to their standard operating procedures, the ASO AQ Plan,
 and the Analytical Service Request (ASR). Samples were analyzed directly (no preparation) by
 GEA.

Test Conditions 8

 4.0 Results
 This section discusses the Cs exchange behavior during batch contact testing with variable Na
 AN-107 and AP-105 tank waste. Batch contact raw data are provided in Appendix A.

 4.1 Kd and isotherm results
 Figure 4-1 shows the Kd dependence on Cs concentration in AN-107 at various Na
 concentrations. The Kd increased with decreasing Na concentration. This result is expected as
 Na competes directly with Cs for CST sites (Campbell 2023). The data show negligible changes
 in the Kd for the three lower Cs concentrations (1.7E-04 M, 4.4E-04 M, and 1.0E-03 M) measured.
 This behavior has been observed for AP-105 (Westesen 2023) and suggests that there is no
 impact on Kd with small changes in Cs concentrations of <1E-03 M Cs. For the lower Cs
 concentration samples at 6.0 M Na, there is a significant change in Kd between the duplicate
 measurements. Also at the lower Cs concentrations, the 7.0 M Na samples show a slightly lower
 Kd than the 8.0 M Na samples. These results are likely just associated with analytical uncertainty
 in the Kd measurements and should not be taken as a significant deviation. Rather, trends should
 be assessed across the entirety of the data set to evaluate the impact of changing Na
 concentrations on CST performance.

 The results for both tanks show a decreasing trend in Cs loadings (Q values) with increasing Na
 concentrations. This can be attributed reduced ionic strength and decreased competitive ion
 effects as a result of sample dilution. For the AN-107 tank, the 7.0 M Na model shows lower Cs
 loadings than the 8.0 M Na model. This is consistent with the Kd values recorded; the trend is
 attributed to analytical uncertainty and considered negligible.

 4.2 Tank waste comparisons
 Batch contact studies were conducted on AN-107 and AP-105 (this work) and AP-107 (Campbell
 2023) to assess Cs removal at variable Na concentrations. Table 4-1 shows a comparison of the
 Kd and Q values for CST in the three tank samples; data is normalized to Na concentrations in
 AN-107. For all tank wastes, both Kd and Q values show a general decreasing trend with
 increasing Na concentration as expected with increasing ionic strength. The AN-107 data show
 higher Kd values than either AP-105 or AP-107. This is due to the lower potassium concentration
 in this sample. The data for AP-107 and AP-105 overlap – indicating that there are nominal
 separations between these two tanks. Prior column testing has demonstrated that CST has a

Results 12

 slightly greater capacity for cesium in the AP-107 matrix (implying slightly higher Kd values), but
 this is difference is difficult to assess solely from batch contact tests. It is interesting to note that
 the AN-107 sample shows a much greater dependence on sodium loading. The cesium loading
 varies by more than a factor of 2 between 3.5 M and 8 M. This is assessed by multiplying the
 sodium molarity by the Kd. In contrast, AP-105 and AP-107 showed roughly a 30% decrease in
 cesium capacity. Again, this is likely associated with the much lower potassium content in the
 AN-107 sample but should be validated with other low potassium matrices. These changes are
 due to the changes in activity coefficients as a function of the ionic strength of the solution (as a
 result of dilution) and the mix of anions that are present. Prior work has shown that the cesium
 activity coefficient is impacted more by increases in ionic strength than the sodium activity
 coefficient. This non-ideality results in lower effective cesium loading at higher ionic strength.

          7.0    9.43E-05    353      0.030     8.25E-05    589      0.054     8.97.E-05     594      0.055

          8.0    1.13E-04    342      0.043     1.00E-04    466      0.053     1.03.E-04     419      0.045

Results 13

 5.0 Conclusions
 A comparative analysis of batch contact testing was conducted for AN-107 and AP-105 samples
 at various Na and Cs concentrations. Batch contacts were conducted in duplicate with 0.075 g
 dry CST (Lot No. 2002009604) per 15 mL of solution and agitated at ambient temperature for an
 average of ~240 hours. The isotherm data were fit to the Freundlich/Langmuir hybrid equilibrium
 model to calculate Kd and Q values. These results were compared to AP-107 data. The following
 conclusions were made from this testing:

 1. For all tank wastes, the data suggests CST’s selectivity and capacity for Cs removal are
 more pronounced in scenarios with lower Na concentrations; this is influenced by the
 overall lower ionic strength of the tank waste samples and the impact on activity
 coefficients associated with these changes in ionic strength.

 2. All tank wastes exhibited decreasing Kd values with increasing Na concentration,
 indicating the influence of competitive ion presence on the CST’s affinity for Cs.

 3. AN-107 showed generally higher Kd and Q values across all tested Na concentrations
 compared to AP-105. The differences are primarily due to the lower potassium in AN-107.

 4. AP-105 and AP-107 showed similar Kd values, however prior column testing has
 demonstrated that CST has a slightly higher affinity for cesium in the AP-107 matrix.

15.1) C0962 ASR-2094 Branch Set 2 Customer Report Page 1 of 4

                                                                                              Appendix A1054 of 2000

Battelle PNNL/RPL/Inorganic Analysis … ICP-OES Analysis Report

Six liquid samples for Set 2 were submitted under Analytical Service Request (ASR) 2094 and
were analyzed by ICP-OES. The samples had an acid digestion performed by the Radiochemistry
team.

All sample results are reported on a mass per mass basis (µg/g) for each detected analyte. The
data have been adjusted for instrument dilutions.

Analytes of interest (AOI) were specified in the ASR and are listed in the highlighted section of
the attached ICP-OES Data Report. The quality control (QC) results for the AOI have been
evaluated and are presented below. The current AOI for this run (C0962) are Potassium (K) and
Sodium (Na).

Samples were prepared by radiochemistry team by first digesting in aqua regia to fully digest the
organic material and taken to soft dryness. Following this, samples were converted to 2% HNO3
and again taken to soft dryness.

Limited Data:
Tungsten, and Tin is for information only and may be biased high. Strontium is for information
only and may be biased low.

Calibration of the ICP-OES was done following the manufacturer’s recommended calibration
procedure using multi-analyte custom standard solutions traceable to the National Institute of
Standards and Technology (NIST). Midrange calibration verification standards (MCVA and
MCVB) were used to verify acceptance of the two-point calibration curves obtained for each
analyte and for continuing calibration verification.

The controlling documents were procedures RPG-CMC-211, Rev 4, Determination of Elemental
Composition by Inductively Coupled Argon Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES),
and ASO-QAP-001, Rev. 11, Analytical Support Operations (ASO) Quality Assurance Plan.
Instrument calibrations, QC checks and blanks (e.g., ICV/ICB, CCV/CCB, LLS, ICS), post-
digestion spikes, duplicate, blank spike, and serial dilution were conducted during the analysis
run.

Preparation Blank (PB):
 A preparation blank was supplied with the samples by the radiochemistry team. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criteria of <EQL (estimated quantitation level), <50%
 regulatory decision level, or less than 5% of the concentration in the sample.

Blank Spike (BS)/Laboratory Control Sample (LCS):
 A 50:50 mixture of the MCVA and MCVB solutions was analyzed as the blank spike.
 Recovery values are listed for all analytes included in the BS that were measured at or
 above the EQL. All AOI meeting this requirement were within the acceptance criteria of
     80% to 120%.

 For 24-2288 BS @1x, all AOI included in the spike were within the acceptance criteria.

15.1) C0962 ASR-2094 Branch Set 2 Customer Report Page 2 of 4

                                                                                              Appendix A1055 of 2000

Battelle PNNL/RPL/Inorganic Analysis … ICP-OES Analysis Report

Duplicate/Replicate Relative Percent Difference (RPD):
 A duplicate of sample 24-2288 Dup @10x was prepared and analyzed. RPD are listed for
 all analytes that were measured at or above the EQL. All AOI detected were within the
 acceptance criterion of ≤20% for liquid samples.

Matrix-Spike (MS) Sample:
 A matrix spike sample was created during sample preparation beforehand by the
 radiochemistry team.

 For 24-2288 MS @10x, Potassium passed within the range of acceptance, but Sodium was
 an invalid test due the spike being less than 25% of sample concentration.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Verification (ICV/CCV):
 MCVA and MCVB solutions were analyzed immediately after calibration, after each group
 of not more than ten samples, and at the end of the analytical run. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 90% to 110%.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Blank (ICB/CCB):
 The ICB/CCB solution (5% v/v HNO3) was analyzed immediately after the ICV solutions
 and after the CCV solutions (after each group of not more than ten samples and at the end
 of the analytical run). All AOI passed on the ICB/CCBs.

Low-Level Standard (LLS):
 The LLS solution was analyzed immediately after the first CCB solution. All AOI were
 within the acceptance criteria of 70% to 130%.

Interference Check Standard (ICS/SST):
 The ICS solution was analyzed immediately after the first LLS solution and immediately
 prior to analyzing the final CCV solutions. Recovery values are listed for all analytes
 included in the SST that were measured at or above the EQL. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 80% to 120%.

Serial Dilution (SD):
 A five-fold serial dilution was conducted on sample 24-2292 @50x. The percent difference
 (%D) for Na was withing the acceptance criteria of ≤ 10%. K was not with a percent
 difference of 10.2%. This issues is likely due to K concentration being at the bottom of the
 calibration range.

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-A) - Sample (A Component):
 A post-digestion spike (A Component) was conducted on sample 24-2289 @50x. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criterion of 80% to 120%.

Battelle PNNL/RPL/Inorganic Analysis … ICP-OES Analysis Report

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-B) - Sample (B Component):
 A post-digestion spike (B Component) was conducted on sample 24-2290 @50x. No AOI
 were present in the PS-B spike, but all other analytes passed within the PS-B spike.

Other QC:
 All other instrument-related QC tests for the AOI passed within their respective acceptance
 criteria.

Comments:
 1) The “Final Results” have been corrected for all laboratory dilutions performed on the samples during
 processing and analysis, unless specifically noted.
 2) Instrument detection limits (IDL) and estimated quantitation limits (EQL) shown are for acidified water
 and/or fusion flux matrices as applicable. Method detection limits (MDL) for individual samples can be
 estimated by multiplying the IDL by the “Process Factor” for that individual sample. The estimated
 quantitation limit (EQL) for each concentration value can be obtained by multiplying the EQL by the
 “Process Factor”.
 3) Routine precision and bias is typically ±15% or better for samples in dilute, acidified water (e.g. 5% v/v
 HNO3 or less) at analyte concentrations > EQL up to the upper calibration level. This also presumes that
 the total dissolved solids concentration in the sample is less than 5000 g/mL (0.5 per cent by weight).
 Note that bracketed values listed in the data report are within the MDL and the EQL, and have potential
 uncertainties greater than 15%. Concentration values < MDL are listed as “- -”. Note, that calibration and
 QC standard samples are validated to a precision of ±10%.
 4) Analytes included in the spike MCVA component (for the AS/PS) are; Ag, Al, As, B, Ba, Be, Bi, Ca, Cd,
 Co, Cr, Cu, Eu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Mo, Na, Ni, P, Pb, Sb, Se, Si, Sm, Sn, Sr, Ta, Ti, Tl, V, W, Y, Zn, and
 Zr. Analytes included in the spike MCVB component are; Ce, Dy, Eu, La, Nd, Pd, Rh, Ru, S, Te, Th, and
 U.

Battelle PNNL/RPL/Inorganic Analysis … ICP-OES Analysis Report

Six liquid samples for Set 1 were submitted under Analytical Service Request (ASR) 2120 and
were analyzed by ICP-OES. The samples had an acid digestion performed by the Radiochemistry
team.

All sample results are reported on a mass per mass basis (µg/g) for each detected analyte. The
data have been adjusted for instrument dilutions.

Analytes of interest (AOI) were specified in the ASR and are listed in the highlighted section of
the attached ICP-OES Data Report. The quality control (QC) results for the AOI have been
evaluated and are presented below. The current AOI for this run (C0965) are Potassium (K) and
Sodium (Na).

Samples were prepared by radiochemistry team by first digesting in aqua regia to fully digest the
organic material and taken to soft dryness. Following this, samples were converted to 0.5M
HNO3 and again taken to soft dryness.

Limited Data:
Data for Lithium, Tungsten, and Tin is for information only and may be biased high due to
failing QC checks high.

Calibration of the ICP-OES was done following the manufacturer’s recommended calibration
procedure using multi-analyte custom standard solutions traceable to the National Institute of
Standards and Technology (NIST). Midrange calibration verification standards (MCVA and
MCVB) were used to verify acceptance of the two-point calibration curves obtained for each
analyte and for continuing calibration verification.

The controlling documents were procedures RPG-CMC-211, Rev 4, Determination of Elemental
Composition by Inductively Coupled Argon Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES),
and ASO-QAP-001, Rev. 11, Analytical Support Operations (ASO) Quality Assurance Plan.
Instrument calibrations, QC checks and blanks (e.g., ICV/ICB, CCV/CCB, LLS, ICS), post-
digestion spikes, duplicate, blank spike, and serial dilution were conducted during the analysis
run.

Preparation Blank (PB):
 A preparation blank was supplied with the samples by the radiochemistry team. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criteria of <EQL (estimated quantitation level), <50%
 regulatory decision level, or less than 5% of the concentration in the sample.

Blank Spike (BS)/Laboratory Control Sample (LCS):
 A 50:50 mixture of the MCVA and MCVB solutions was analyzed as the blank spike.
 Recovery values are listed for all analytes included in the BS that were measured at or
 above the EQL. All AOI meeting this requirement were within the acceptance criteria of
     80% to 120%.

 For 24-2495 BS @1x, all AOI included in the spike were within the acceptance criteria.

ASR-2120 Branch Set 1 Customer Report Page 2 of 4

                                                                                              Appendix A1991 of 2000

Battelle PNNL/RPL/Inorganic Analysis … ICP-OES Analysis Report

Duplicate/Replicate Relative Percent Difference (RPD):
 A duplicate of sample 24-2495 Dup @10x was prepared and analyzed. All AOI detected
 were within the acceptance criterion of ≤20% for liquid samples with RPD of 2.6 for K and
 1.1 for Na.

Matrix-Spike (MS) Sample:
 A matrix spike sample was created during sample preparation beforehand by the
 radiochemistry team.

 For 24-2495 MS @10x, Potassium passed within the range of acceptance, but Sodium was
 an invalid test due the spike being less than 25% of sample concentration.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Verification (ICV/CCV):
 MCVA and MCVB solutions were analyzed immediately after calibration, after each group
 of not more than ten samples, and at the end of the analytical run. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 90% to 110%.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Blank (ICB/CCB):
 The ICB/CCB solution (5% v/v HNO3) was analyzed immediately after the ICV solutions
 and after the CCV solutions (after each group of not more than ten samples and at the end
 of the analytical run). All AOI passed on the ICB/CCBs.

Low-Level Standard (LLS):
 The LLS solution was analyzed immediately after the first CCB solution. All AOI were
 within the acceptance criteria of 70% to 130%.

Interference Check Standard (ICS/SST):
 The ICS solution was analyzed immediately after the first LLS solution and immediately
 prior to analyzing the final CCV solutions. Recovery values are listed for all analytes
 included in the SST that were measured at or above the EQL. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 80% to 120%.

Serial Dilution (SD):
 A five-fold serial dilution was conducted on sample 24-2495 @50x. The percent difference
 (%D) for Na and K was withing the acceptance criteria of ≤ 10%.

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-A) - Sample (A Component):
 A post-digestion spike (A Component) was conducted on sample 24-2496 @50x. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criterion of 80% to 120%.

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-B) - Sample (B Component):
 A post-digestion spike (B Component) was conducted on sample 24-2497 @50x. No AOI
 were present in the PSB spike, but all other analytes passed within the PSB spike.

Other QC:
 All other instrument-related QC tests for the AOI passed within their respective acceptance

Comments:
 1) The “Final Results” have been corrected for all laboratory dilutions performed on the samples during
 processing and analysis, unless specifically noted.
 2) Instrument detection limits (IDL) and estimated quantitation limits (EQL) shown are for acidified water
 and/or fusion flux matrices as applicable. Method detection limits (MDL) for individual samples can be
 estimated by multiplying the IDL by the “Process Factor” for that individual sample. The estimated
 quantitation limit (EQL) for each concentration value can be obtained by multiplying the EQL by the
 “Process Factor”.
 3) Routine precision and bias is typically ±15% or better for samples in dilute, acidified water (e.g. 5% v/v
 HNO3 or less) at analyte concentrations > EQL up to the upper calibration level. This also presumes that
 the total dissolved solids concentration in the sample is less than 5000 g/mL (0.5 per cent by weight).
 Note that bracketed values listed in the data report are within the MDL and the EQL, and have potential
 uncertainties greater than 15%. Concentration values < MDL are listed as “- -”. Note, that calibration and
 QC standard samples are validated to a precision of ±10%.
 4) Analytes included in the spike MCVA component (for the AS/PS) are; Ag, Al, As, B, Ba, Be, Bi, Ca, Cd,
 Co, Cr, Cu, Eu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Mo, Na, Ni, P, Pb, Sb, Se, Si, Sm, Sn, Sr, Ta, Ti, Tl, V, W, Y, Zn, and
 Zr. Analytes included in the spike MCVB component are; Ce, Dy, Eu, La, Nd, Pd, Rh, Ru, S, Te, Th, and
 U.

                                                                                              Appendix A1996 of 2000

Six liquid samples for Set 2 were submitted under Analytical Service Request (ASR) 2120 and
were analyzed by ICP-OES. The samples had an acid digestion performed by the Radiochemistry
team.

All sample results are reported on a mass per mass basis (µg/g) for each detected analyte. The
data have been adjusted for instrument dilutions.

Analytes of interest (AOI) were specified in the ASR and are listed in the highlighted section of
the attached ICP-OES Data Report. The quality control (QC) results for the AOI have been
evaluated and are presented below. The current AOI for this run (C0966) are Potassium (K) and
Sodium (Na).

Samples were prepared by radiochemistry team by first digesting in aqua regia to fully digest the
organic material and taken to soft dryness. Following this, samples were converted to 0.5M
HNO3 and again taken to soft dryness.

Limited Data:
Data for Cadmium, Lithium, Selenium, Strontium, Tungsten, and Tin is for information only and
may be biased high due to failing QC checks high.

Calibration of the ICP-OES was done following the manufacturer’s recommended calibration
procedure using multi-analyte custom standard solutions traceable to the National Institute of
Standards and Technology (NIST). Midrange calibration verification standards (MCVA and
MCVB) were used to verify acceptance of the two-point calibration curves obtained for each
analyte and for continuing calibration verification.

The controlling documents were procedures RPG-CMC-211, Rev 4, Determination of Elemental
Composition by Inductively Coupled Argon Plasma Optical Emission Spectrometry (ICP-OES),
and ASO-QAP-001, Rev. 11, Analytical Support Operations (ASO) Quality Assurance Plan.
Instrument calibrations, QC checks and blanks (e.g., ICV/ICB, CCV/CCB, LLS, ICS), post-
digestion spikes, duplicate, blank spike, and serial dilution were conducted during the analysis
run.

Preparation Blank (PB):
 A preparation blank was supplied with the samples by the radiochemistry team. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criteria of <EQL (estimated quantitation level), <50%
 regulatory decision level, or less than ≤5% of the concentration in the sample.

Blank Spike (BS)/Laboratory Control Sample (LCS):
 A 50:50 mixture of the MCVA and MCVB solutions was analyzed as the blank spike.
 Recovery values are listed for all analytes included in the BS that were measured at or
 above the EQL. All AOI meeting this requirement were within the acceptance criteria of
     80% to 120%.

 For 24-2501 BS @1x, all AOI included in the spike were within the acceptance criteria.

                                                                                              Appendix A1997 of 2000

Duplicate/Replicate Relative Percent Difference (RPD):
 A duplicate of sample 24-2501 Dup @10x was prepared and analyzed. All AOI detected
 were within the acceptance criterion of ≤20% for liquid samples with RPD of 0.1 for K and
 1.4 for Na.

Matrix-Spike (MS) Sample:
 A matrix spike sample was created during sample preparation beforehand by the
 radiochemistry team.

 For 24-2501 MS @10x, Potassium passed within the range of acceptance, but Sodium was
 an invalid test due the spike being less than 25% of sample concentration.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Verification (ICV/CCV):
 MCVA and MCVB solutions were analyzed immediately after calibration, after each group
 of not more than ten samples, and at the end of the analytical run. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 90% to 110%.

Initial/Continuing Calibration Blank (ICB/CCB):
 The ICB/CCB solution (5% v/v HNO3) was analyzed immediately after the ICV solutions
 and after the CCV solutions (after each group of not more than ten samples and at the end
 of the analytical run). All AOI passed on the ICB/CCBs.

Low-Level Standard (LLS):
 The LLS solution was analyzed immediately after the first CCB solution. All AOI were
 within the acceptance criteria of 70% to 130%.

Interference Check Standard (ICS/SST):
 The ICS solution was analyzed immediately after the first LLS solution and immediately
 prior to analyzing the final CCV solutions. Recovery values are listed for all analytes
 included in the SST that were measured at or above the EQL. All AOI were within the
 acceptance criteria of 80% to 120%.

Serial Dilution (SD):
 A five-fold serial dilution was conducted on sample 24-2501 @50x. The percent difference
 (%D) for Na and K was withing the acceptance criteria of ≤ 10%.

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-A) - Sample (A Component):
 A post-digestion spike (A Component) was conducted on sample 24-2502 @50x. All AOI
 were within the acceptance criterion of 80% to 120%.

Post-Digestion Spike (PS-B) - Sample (B Component):
 A post-digestion spike (B Component) was conducted on sample 24-2503 @50x. No AOI
 were present in the PSB spike, but all other analytes passed within the PSB spike.

                                                                                                          Appendix A1998 of 2000

Other QC:
 All other instrument-related QC tests for the AOI passed within their respective acceptance
 criteria.

Comments:
 1) The “Final Results” have been corrected for all laboratory dilutions performed on the samples during
 processing and analysis, unless specifically noted.
 2) Instrument detection limits (IDL) and estimated quantitation limits (EQL) shown are for acidified water
 and/or fusion flux matrices as applicable. Method detection limits (MDL) for individual samples can be
 estimated by multiplying the IDL by the “Process Factor” for that individual sample. The estimated
 quantitation limit (EQL) for each concentration value can be obtained by multiplying the EQL by the
 “Process Factor”.
 3) Routine precision and bias is typically ±15% or better for samples in dilute, acidified water (e.g. 5% v/v
 HNO3 or less) at analyte concentrations > EQL up to the upper calibration level. This also presumes that
 the total dissolved solids concentration in the sample is less than 5000 µg/mL (0.5 per cent by weight).
 Note that bracketed values listed in the data report are within the MDL and the EQL, and have potential
 uncertainties greater than 15%. Concentration values < MDL are listed as “- -”. Note, that calibration and
 QC standard samples are validated to a precision of ±10%.
 4) Analytes included in the spike MCVA component (for the AS/PS) are; Ag, Al, As, B, Ba, Be, Bi, Ca, Cd,
 Co, Cr, Cu, Eu, Fe, K, Li, Mg, Mn, Mo, Na, Ni, P, Pb, Sb, Se, Si, Sm, Sn, Sr, Ta, Ti, Tl, V, W, Y, Zn, and
 Zr. Analytes included in the spike MCVB component are; Ce, Dy, Eu, La, Nd, Pd, Rh, Ru, S, Te, Th, and
 U.
